nameStory: The Eastern Meadow Vole gets its name from its favorite hangout spots — open meadows, grasslands, and fields where it scurries through the tall grass. 'Vole' comes from an old Norwegian word meaning 'field,' which perfectly describes where you're most likely to spot these busy little rodents. You might also hear them called 'meadow mice' or 'field mice,' though they're not true mice at all!
description: The Eastern Meadow Vole is a chunky, compact rodent about the size of a computer mouse, typically 3-5 inches long with a short tail that's less than half its body length. These brown, furry creatures have small ears that barely peek above their dense fur, tiny dark eyes, and a blunt snout perfect for munching grass. They're built low to the ground with short legs, making them look like little furry sausages as they dart through meadows and fields. Despite their mouse-like appearance, voles are stockier and have much shorter tails than true mice.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact, chunky body about 3-5 inches long with a distinctly short tail (less than 2 inches) that's much shorter than the body length. The body feels solid and dense if handled, unlike the more delicate build of a house mouse.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, soft fur that ranges from grayish-brown to rich chocolate brown on top, with lighter gray or buff-colored belly. The fur has a slightly coarse texture when touched and often appears grizzled or salt-and-pepper colored up close.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny four-toed front prints and five-toed hind prints, each less than half an inch long. Look for paired prints in snow or mud, often leading to or from tunnel entrances in grass.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Creates distinctive runways or tunnels through grass that feel springy underfoot. Active day and night, making rustling sounds in tall grass as they move quickly along their hidden pathways.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for pencil-thick tunnels through matted grass, small piles of green grass clippings, and tiny rice-sized droppings scattered along runways. Grass stems show clean, angled cuts about an inch above ground level.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found in areas with dense grass cover — avoid bare ground and prefer thick vegetation they can tunnel through. Unlike mice, rarely seen climbing or in buildings.

habitat: Eastern Meadow Voles thrive in any area with dense, continuous grass cover throughout New England — from abandoned fields and prairie remnants to marshy meadows and even unmowed sections of parks and cemeteries. They prefer areas where grass grows thick enough to create a canopy over their tunnel systems, including wet meadows, field edges, and grassy ditches. You'll find their runway systems in both lowland areas and mountain meadows up to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Most active time for spotting voles as they emerge from winter tunnels and begin breeding. Look for fresh runway construction and increased rustling in newly green grass.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with multiple generations being born. Runways are most visible and extensive, and you might catch glimpses of young voles learning to navigate the tunnel systems.
seasonality.fall: Voles work frantically to prepare winter food caches, cutting and storing grass stems. Their runways expand as they gather materials for insulation and food storage.
seasonality.winter: Activity continues under snow cover where they create an elaborate tunnel system between the ground and snow. Look for entrance holes in snow and scattered droppings on the surface after snowmelt.

funFact: A single meadow vole can create over 100 feet of interconnected grass tunnels in just one season, essentially building an underground highway system complete with multiple bedrooms, pantries, and emergency exits — all without ever needing to surface and expose themselves to predators!
confusionNotes: Often confused with house mice, but remember the simple rule: short tail = vole, long tail = mouse. If the tail is shorter than the body, you've got a vole; if it's longer than the body, it's a mouse. Voles also have much smaller ears and eyes relative to their head size.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'meadow mice' or 'field mice,' these aren't actually mice at all — they're more closely related to hamsters and lemmings. This naming confusion has persisted for generations, so don't be surprised when locals use these interchangeable terms for the same little tunnel-maker.
compareHints: The Eastern Meadow Vole is larger and prefers more open, grassy areas compared to its cousin the Woodland Vole, which is smaller and sticks to forested areas with loose soil for burrowing underground. While Meadow Voles build surface runways through grass, Woodland Voles create deeper tunnel systems and are rarely seen above ground. Meadow Voles also have slightly longer tails and lighter-colored fur than their woodland relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Woodland voles are much more secretive than Eastern meadow voles, which are commonly seen scurrying through grass in daylight.
